suggestions.rationale: Depression is associated with gout at the population level, but the available evidence does not establish that gout caused or aggravated an individual's depressive disorder. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies reported a pooled odds ratio of 1.29 for depression among people with gout and, across four incidence studies, a pooled hazard ratio of 1.17 for incident depression. Flare frequency, tophi, pain, disability, comorbidity, medication exposure, sleep, and psychiatric history still require case-specific review before any individual secondary theory is considered.
evidenceGaps: Rheumatology or primary-care documentation confirming gout phenotype, flare burden, tophi, pain, and functional impact
Depressive-disorder diagnosis, severity, and chronology relative to gout onset and flares
Cardiometabolic, renal, sleep, medication, pain, disability, and psychosocial contributors
History of depressive symptoms predating gout or another independent psychiatric disorder
Qualified clinician assessment distinguishing population-level gout/depression association from individual causation or aggravation

sourceReferences.citation: Howren A, Bowie D, Choi HK, Rai SK, De Vera MA. Epidemiology of Depression and Anxiety in Gout: A Systematic Review and Metaanalysis. J Rheumatol. 2021;48(1):129-137. PMID 32115430
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 20 studies found a positive association between gout and depression, including pooled OR 1.29 and pooled incident-depression HR 1.17; supports association/comorbidity research, not individual causal attribution.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 32115430; abstract Results/Conclusion: 20 included studies; depression pooled OR 1.29 (95% CI 1.07-1.56); four incidence studies pooled HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.01-1.36)
